---
title: "Case study: compare priors and recovered programs"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Case study: compare priors and recovered programs}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

Do different feature priors change prediction or the programs recovered? This
small simulation has known rank-two signal, sparse signed effects, and repeated
samples from simulated donors. It fits a normal and a sparse (point-Laplace)
effects prior, then compares the two fits three ways: reconstruction against
known truth, held-out prediction by donor, and program agreement. It illustrates
a workflow, not a calibrated benchmark or a recommendation of one prior.
[Get started](first-fit.html) defines view, activity and effects.

```{r data}
library(flashier.utils)
set.seed(31)
metadata <- data.frame(sample = paste0("s", 1:60),
  donor = rep(paste0("d", 1:20), each = 3))
A <- matrix(rnorm(40), 20, 2)[rep(1:20, each = 3), ] +
     matrix(rnorm(120, sd = .2), 60, 2)
B <- matrix(0, 24, 2)
B[1:8, 1] <- rep(c(1, -1), 4)
B[9:16, 2] <- rep(c(1, -1), 4)
signal <- tcrossprod(A, B)
X <- signal + matrix(rnorm(1440, sd = .3), 60, 24)
dimnames(X) <- dimnames(signal) <- list(metadata$sample, paste0("g", 1:24))
priors <- list(normal = list(ebnm::ebnm_normal, ebnm::ebnm_normal),
               sparse = list(ebnm::ebnm_normal, ebnm::ebnm_point_laplace))
fits <- lapply(priors, function(p) {
  set.seed(7)
  flashier::flash(X, greedy_Kmax = 2, ebnm_fn = p,
    nullcheck = FALSE, backfit = TRUE, verbose = 0)
})
views <- lapply(fits, standardize_factors, sample_side = "rows", scaling = "raw",
  feature_scale = "simulated_intensity",
  prior_support = c(activity = "signed", effects = "signed"))
```

```{r effects-figure, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Grid of bar charts, rows F1 and F2, columns truth, normal and sparse. The truth has eight alternating-sign genes per factor; the normal prior gives every one of the 24 genes a nonzero effect; the sparse prior leaves the genes outside each block near zero.", fig.cap="Feature effects per factor (rows) under each fit (columns) for the 24 simulated genes. Simulated intensities, no biology. Factor order and sign are arbitrary across columns; the planted truth is one basis among rotations."}
library(ggplot2)
dimnames(B) <- list(colnames(X), c("F1", "F2"))
effects_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(truth = "truth", names(views)), function(p)
  cbind(fit = p, as.data.frame(as.table(if (p == "truth") B else views[[p]]$effects)))))
names(effects_long)[2:4] <- c("feature", "factor", "effect")
effects_long$fit <- factor(effects_long$fit, c("truth", "normal", "sparse"))
ggplot(effects_long, aes(feature, effect)) + geom_col(fill = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + facet_grid(factor ~ fit) + theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7)) +
  labs(x = "simulated gene", y = "effect (simulated intensity units)")
```

The sparse prior pushes the genes outside each planted block toward zero.
The normal prior gives every gene a small effect. Both reconstruct the
training matrix about equally well, as the next section shows.

## Reconstruction and known signal

Both fits are scored on the training matrix and on the noise-free signal.

```{r reconstruction}
predictions <- lapply(views, function(v)
  sweep(tcrossprod(v$activity, v$effects), 2, v$offset, "+"))
metrics <- function(observed, predicted) {
  c(rmse = sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2)),
    mae = mean(abs(observed - predicted)),
    prediction_r2 = 1 - sum((observed - predicted)^2) /
                          sum((observed - mean(observed))^2))
}
scores <- rbind(normal_training = metrics(X, predictions$normal),
      sparse_training = metrics(X, predictions$sparse),
      normal_truth = metrics(signal, predictions$normal),
      sparse_truth = metrics(signal, predictions$sparse))
vapply(fits, function(f) f$n_factors, numeric(1))
```

```{r reconstruction-figure, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, fig.alt="Grid of bar charts, rows rmse, mae and prediction R squared, columns normal and sparse prior; each panel has a training bar and a truth bar labelled with its value. Corresponding bars are nearly equal across the two columns.", fig.cap="Reconstruction of the training matrix and of the noise-free signal, one fit per matrix (no replicates, so no uncertainty is shown). Simulated data. The two priors are indistinguishable on this criterion."}
scores_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(scores))
names(scores_long) <- c("fit", "metric", "value")
scores_long$prior <- sub("_.*", "", scores_long$fit)
scores_long$target <- sub(".*_", "", scores_long$fit)
ggplot(scores_long, aes(target, value)) + geom_col(fill = "grey30", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 3)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ prior, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  theme_minimal() + labs(x = "scored against", y = NULL)
```

```{r reconstruction-table}
round(scores, 3)
```

Training reconstruction rewards fitting observed noise. Truth recovery is
measurable here because signal was simulated; real-data agreement cannot supply
that truth. Inspect native convergence warnings and failures before ranking.
Native ELBO is not automatically comparable across different prior/noise/objective
settings; maximum ELBO over starts is a different question.

## Identical held-out information

`factor_holdout()` splits donors into folds, refits on training donors, and
scores withheld entries. In masked mode held-out activities are estimated from
`activity_features` only, and prediction is scored on the disjoint
`scoring_features`.

```{r holdout}
folds <- data.frame(donor = paste0("d", 1:20), fold = rep(1:2, each = 10))
results <- lapply(priors, function(p) {
  callback <- function(X, metadata, sample_side, seed, settings, observation_aux) {
    fit_ebmf(X, sample_side = sample_side, ebnm_fn = settings$priors,
      max_factors = 2, backfit = TRUE, nullcheck = FALSE,
      seed = seed, verbose = 0, feature_scale = "simulated_intensity")
  }
  factor_holdout(X, metadata, unit_col = "donor", folds = folds, fit_fn = callback,
    evaluation = "masked", activity_features = paste0("g", c(1:4, 9:12, 17:20)),
    scoring_features = paste0("g", c(5:8, 13:16, 21:24)), seed = 7,
    control = list(sample_side = "rows", settings = list(priors = p),
      preprocessing_manifest = list(scope = "identity"), maxiter = 1000))
})
stopifnot(all(vapply(results, function(r) nrow(r$failures) == 0L, logical(1))))
holdout <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(results), function(p) {
  m <- results[[p]]$metrics
  cbind(prior = p, m[m$weighting == "macro_unit", c("fold", "model", "rmse", "prediction_r2")])
}))
```

```{r holdout-figure, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Grid of dot charts, rows held-out RMSE and prediction R squared, columns normal and sparse prior. In each panel the fitted programs (filled circle) and the training-mean baseline (open triangle) are shown for fold 1 and fold 2. Both priors beat the baseline on both folds by a similar margin.", fig.cap="Held-out prediction per donor fold (10 donors, 30 samples per fold; macro-averaged over donors). Baseline is the training mean of each scoring feature. Two folds give no interval; each point is one refit."}
holdout_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(holdout[, 1:3], metric = "rmse", value = holdout$rmse),
  data.frame(holdout[, 1:3], metric = "prediction_r2", value = holdout$prediction_r2))
ggplot(holdout_long, aes(factor(fold), value, shape = model)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + scale_shape_manual(values = c(fixed_programs = 16, training_mean = 2)) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ prior, scales = "free_y") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "donor fold", y = NULL, shape = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r holdout-table}
holdout
```

Donors never cross folds. Held-out activities use only permitted features; the
same withheld entries score both models and a training-mean baseline. Real learned
preprocessing needs paired training-fit/frozen-transform callbacks. Empirical-Bayes
projection can recalibrate activity priors/noise on permitted query observations;
this is not a fully frozen hyperparameter prediction experiment.

## Program agreement and ambiguity

`factor_replicability()` matches factors across the two fits by Tucker
congruence (cosine similarity of effect vectors) with one-to-one assignment.

```{r alignment}
alignment <- factor_replicability(views$normal, views$sparse, min_congruence = .8)
alignment$matches
```

```{r alignment-figure, fig.width=4, fig.height=3, fig.alt="Two by two heatmap of congruence between normal-prior and sparse-prior factors; the diagonal cells are near one and the off-diagonal cells near zero.", fig.cap="Tucker congruence (cosine of effect vectors over the 24 shared genes) between the two fits. Acceptance threshold is 0.8; numbers are printed so colour is not the only encoding."}
congruence <- as.data.frame(as.table(alignment$congruence_matrix))
names(congruence) <- c("normal", "sparse", "congruence")
ggplot(congruence, aes(sparse, normal, fill = congruence)) + geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(congruence, 2))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#D55E00", mid = "white", high = "#0072B2", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal() + coord_fixed()
```

Inspect unmatched factors, feature coverage, and assignment margins as well as
accepted matches. Assignment is one-to-one: splits/merges require inspecting the
full matrix. Matching effects does not establish equivalent activity units.

Subspace agreement can survive changes in individual factors. Compute an
orthonormal basis using numerical rank, including zero-rank results:

```{r subspaces}
span <- function(M) {
  s <- svd(M)
  rank <- sum(s$d > max(dim(M)) * max(c(s$d, 0)) * .Machine$double.eps)
  s$u[, seq_len(rank), drop = FALSE]
}
projector_distance <- function(left, right) {
  U <- span(left); V <- span(right)
  sqrt(sum((tcrossprod(U) - tcrossprod(V))^2))
}
c(normal_vs_truth = projector_distance(views$normal$effects, B),
  sparse_vs_truth = projector_distance(views$sparse$effects, B))
theta <- pi / 4
R <- matrix(c(cos(theta), -sin(theta), sin(theta), cos(theta)), 2)
rotated_A <- A %*% R
rotated_B <- B %*% t(solve(R))
stopifnot(max(abs(tcrossprod(rotated_A, rotated_B) - signal)) < 1e-10)
c(reconstruction_difference = max(abs(tcrossprod(rotated_A, rotated_B) - signal)),
  subspace_distance = projector_distance(B, rotated_B))
abs(crossprod(B, rotated_B) / sqrt(outer(colSums(B^2), colSums(rotated_B^2))))
```

This rotation preserves signal/subspace exactly, while each pairwise congruence
is about 0.707, below a 0.8 acceptance threshold. Individual-factor disagreement
alone therefore cannot establish lost signal. A broader study must also assess
weak, correlated, overlapping, nonnegative and spurious/missing programs with
repeated seeds and explicit failure accounting.

## Joint coverage of the two program sets

One-to-one matching asks "which factor is which". `compare_prior_fits()` asks a
different question: can each factor of one fit be rebuilt from all factors of
the other? Span coverage allows any signed combination; feasible coverage
respects each factor's declared activity support. Both describe loading
representability only, never program usage or biology.

```{r coverage-figure, fig.width=7, fig.height=3, fig.alt="Two panels, feasible and span. Each shows the uncovered squared loading fraction for reference factors F1 and F2 at their observed poles; all values are near zero.", fig.cap="Uncovered loading fraction of each normal-prior factor when rebuilt from the sparse-prior factors, over the 24 simulated genes. Points are the two observed activity poles (shape and colour); zero means fully representable. Simulated data, one fit per prior, no replication."}
comparison <- compare_prior_fits(views$normal, views$sparse)
plot(comparison, "coverage")
```

```{r coverage-table}
comparison
comparison$coverage[, c("source", "factor", "pole", "span_residual", "feasible_residual", "feasible_status")]
```
